notes.definition: A titration is a method for accurately measuring the volumes of an acid and an alkali that exactly react with each other (neutralise), using an indicator to show the end point. In AQA GCSE Chemistry titrations are carried out with strong acids (hydrochloric, sulfuric and nitric acid) and strong alkalis.
explanation: In a neutralisation reaction, hydrogen ions from the acid react with hydroxide ions from the alkali to make water: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l). A titration lets you find exactly what volume of one solution reacts with a known volume of the other. You cannot see this reaction happening, because both solutions and the products are colourless, so an indicator is added. The end point is the moment the indicator changes colour, showing the alkali has just been neutralised.

The apparatus is chosen for accuracy. A volumetric pipette (used with a pipette filler) measures a fixed volume, usually 25.0 cm³, of alkali into a conical flask. A burette measures the volume of acid added, to the nearest 0.05 cm³. The conical flask can be swirled without spilling, and it stands on a white tile so the colour change is easy to see. A measuring cylinder is not accurate enough for a titration.

A suitable indicator gives a single, sharp colour change. Phenolphthalein is pink in alkali and colourless in acid. Methyl orange is yellow in alkali and red in acid. Universal indicator is not used because it changes colour gradually through many colours, so there is no clear end point.

Method outline: rinse the burette with the acid, fill it, and record the starting reading at eye level from the bottom of the meniscus. Pipette 25.0 cm³ of alkali into a conical flask and add a few drops of indicator. Run in acid while swirling. Near the end point add the acid drop by drop until the indicator just changes colour permanently, then record the final reading. The titre is the final reading minus the initial reading.

The first titration is a rough (trial) run to find the approximate end point. The titration is then repeated, adding acid quickly to about 1 cm³ before the rough end point and then drop by drop. Repeats continue until you have concordant titres, which are results within 0.10 cm³ of each other. The mean titre is calculated from the concordant results only, ignoring the rough titre and any anomalous results.

Higher tier students must use the reacting volumes to calculate concentrations. If the concentration of one solution is known, you can find the number of moles in the volume used (moles = concentration × volume in dm³), use the balanced equation to find the moles of the other reactant, then divide by its volume in dm³ to get its concentration in mol/dm³. Multiplying mol/dm³ by the relative formula mass converts it to g/dm³.
keyFacts: Titrations measure the volumes of acid and alkali that exactly react with each other.
AQA titrations use strong acids (hydrochloric, sulfuric, nitric) and strong alkalis only.
A pipette measures 25.0 cm³ of alkali accurately; a burette measures the volume of acid added.
Read the burette at eye level from the bottom of the meniscus, to the nearest 0.05 cm³.
Phenolphthalein: pink in alkali, colourless in acid. Methyl orange: yellow in alkali, red in acid.
Universal indicator is not suitable because its colour change is gradual.
Titre = final burette reading − initial burette reading.
Concordant titres are within 0.10 cm³ of each other; average only these.
1 dm³ = 1000 cm³, so divide a volume in cm³ by 1000 to get dm³.
Higher: moles = concentration (mol/dm³) × volume (dm³); g/dm³ = mol/dm³ × Mr.

keyTerms.definition: A technique for finding the exact volumes of two solutions that react together, such as an acid and an alkali.
A long graduated tube with a tap, used to add a measured, variable volume of solution to the nearest 0.05 cm³.
A volumetric pipette delivers one fixed volume (for example 25.0 cm³) very accurately; it is filled using a pipette filler.
A substance that changes colour depending on whether a solution is acidic or alkaline.
The point in a titration when the indicator changes colour, showing that the reaction is just complete.
The volume of solution added from the burette to reach the end point.
Titres that are within 0.10 cm³ of each other.
The amount of solute in a given volume of solution, measured in g/dm³ or (Higher) mol/dm³.

equations.name: Titre
equations.formula: titre = final burette reading − initial burette reading

equations.name: Concentration (mass)
equations.formula: concentration (g/dm³) = mass of solute (g) ÷ volume of solution (dm³)

equations.name: Concentration (moles), Higher
equations.formula: concentration (mol/dm³) = number of moles of solute ÷ volume of solution (dm³)

workedExamples.title: Choosing concordant titres and finding the mean
workedExamples.question: A student's titres were: rough 24.10 cm³, run 1 23.60 cm³, run 2 23.15 cm³, run 3 23.25 cm³. Calculate the mean titre.
steps: Ignore the rough titre: it is only a guide.
Look for results within 0.10 cm³ of each other: 23.15 and 23.25 cm³ differ by exactly 0.10 cm³, so they are concordant.
23.60 cm³ is not within 0.10 cm³ of either, so leave it out.

workedExamples.title: Higher: concentration of sodium hydroxide (1 : 1 ratio)
workedExamples.question: 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution was neutralised by 22.50 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide in mol/dm³ and in g/dm³. (Mr of NaOH = 40)
steps: Convert volumes to dm³: 22.50 cm³ = 0.02250 dm³; 25.0 cm³ = 0.0250 dm³.
The ratio HCl : NaOH is 1 : 1, so moles of NaOH = 0.00225 mol.

workedExamples.title: Higher: concentration of sulfuric acid (1 : 2 ratio)
workedExamples.question: 20.00 cm³ of sulfuric acid exactly neutralised 25.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide. H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the sulfuric acid in mol/dm³ and g/dm³. (Mr of H₂SO₄ = 98)
steps: From the equation, 1 mol H₂SO₄ reacts with 2 mol NaOH, so moles of H₂SO₄ = 0.00500 ÷ 2 = 0.00250 mol.
In g/dm³: 0.125 × 98 = 12.25 g/dm³ (12.3 g/dm³ to 3 significant figures).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a measuring cylinder is accurate enough to measure the alkali.
misconceptions.right: In fact a volumetric pipette is used because it delivers 25.0 cm³ far more accurately than a measuring cylinder.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the mean titre should include every result, including the rough one.
misconceptions.right: In fact only concordant titres (within 0.10 cm³ of each other) are averaged; the rough titre and anomalies are left out.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think universal indicator is the best indicator because it shows the pH.
misconceptions.right: In fact universal indicator changes colour gradually, so the end point is unclear. A single-colour-change indicator such as phenolphthalein or methyl orange is used.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the burette should be rinsed with distilled water just before filling it.
misconceptions.right: In fact it is rinsed with the acid it will hold. Water left inside would dilute the acid and make the titre too large.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often use volumes in cm³ directly in concentration calculations.
misconceptions.right: In fact concentration in mol/dm³ needs the volume in dm³, so divide cm³ by 1000 first.

realWorld: Food and drink manufacturers use titrations to check the acidity of products such as vinegar, wine and fruit juice for quality control.
Water companies and environmental scientists use titrations to measure the concentration of substances in water samples.
Pharmaceutical companies use titrations to check that medicines contain the correct amount of an active ingredient.
higherTier: Calculate the chemical quantities in titrations involving concentrations in mol/dm³ and in g/dm³.
Required practical 2 (Higher): determine the concentration of one of the solutions in mol/dm³ and g/dm³ from the reacting volumes and the known concentration of the other solution.
Method: moles of known solution = concentration × volume (dm³); use the balanced equation ratio to find moles of the other substance; concentration = moles ÷ volume (dm³); g/dm³ = mol/dm³ × Mr.
separateOnlyContent: Titrations (4.4.2.5) and required practical 2 are in separate Chemistry (8462) only, not Combined Science Trilogy.
Describe how to carry out titrations using strong acids and strong alkalis only (sulfuric, hydrochloric and nitric acids) to find the reacting volumes accurately.
examTips: When describing the method, name the apparatus precisely: pipette (with filler) for the alkali, burette for the acid, conical flask, white tile.
Always say 'add the acid drop by drop near the end point' and 'swirl the flask': these are common marking points.
Record burette readings to 2 decimal places, ending in 0 or 5 (for example 23.15 cm³).
In calculations, write out each step: moles of known, ratio from the equation, moles of unknown, then concentration. Method marks are given even if the final answer is wrong.
Check the equation ratio for sulfuric acid: H₂SO₄ reacts with 2NaOH, so halve (or double) the moles.
summary: A titration finds the exact volumes of acid and alkali that react.
Use a pipette for 25.0 cm³ of alkali, a burette for the acid, and a single-colour-change indicator.
Add acid drop by drop near the end point, swirling, until the indicator just changes colour.
Repeat until titres are concordant (within 0.10 cm³) and average those.
Higher: use moles = concentration × volume and the equation ratio to find an unknown concentration in mol/dm³ and g/dm³.

questions.question: A student needs to put exactly 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution into a conical flask for a titration. Which piece of apparatus should they use?
questions.explanation: A volumetric pipette delivers one fixed volume very accurately. A measuring cylinder and a beaker are far less accurate. A burette is used for the solution being added during the titration, not for measuring the alkali into the flask.

options: To make the colour change of the indicator easier to see
To stop the flask from getting hot
To make the reaction happen faster
markScheme: 1 mark: to make the colour change easier to see
questions.explanation: The white background makes it easy to spot the exact moment the indicator changes colour. The tile has no effect on temperature or rate of reaction.

questions.question: Why is universal indicator not used in a titration?
options: It does not work with strong acids
It changes colour gradually, so the end point is not sharp
markScheme: 1 mark: gradual colour change so no clear end point
questions.explanation: Universal indicator passes through many colours as pH changes, so it is hard to tell the exact end point. It does work with strong acids; the problem is the gradual change, not a reaction or cost.

questions.question: What colour is phenolphthalein indicator in sodium hydroxide solution?
questions.explanation: Phenolphthalein is pink in alkali and colourless in acid. Yellow is the colour of methyl orange in alkali, and red is methyl orange in acid.

questions.question: Which set of titres contains two concordant results?
questions.explanation: Concordant titres are within 0.10 cm³ of each other. 22.15 − 22.10 = 0.05 cm³, which is within 0.10 cm³. The other pairs differ by 0.20, 0.40 and 0.15 cm³, which are all more than 0.10 cm³.

questions.question: A student adds hydrochloric acid from a burette to sodium hydroxide solution containing methyl orange. What colour change shows the end point?
questions.explanation: Methyl orange is yellow in the alkali at the start. When the alkali is just neutralised and a drop of excess acid is present, it turns red. Red to yellow is the reverse. Pink and colourless are the colours of phenolphthalein, not methyl orange.

questions.question: A student rinses the burette with distilled water and then fills it with acid without rinsing it with acid. What is the effect on the titre?
options: The titre will be smaller, because the acid is more concentrated
There will be no effect on the titre
The indicator will not change colour
The titre will be larger, because the acid has been diluted
markScheme: 1 mark: titre larger because acid diluted
questions.explanation: Water left in the burette dilutes the acid, so each cm³ contains fewer H⁺ ions. More acid must be added to neutralise the alkali, so the titre is larger. The indicator still changes colour.

questions.question: Why should the conical flask be swirled while the acid is being added?
options: To speed up evaporation of water
To mix the acid and alkali so they react fully
To make the indicator more concentrated
questions.explanation: Swirling mixes the acid into the alkali so the indicator shows the true colour of the whole solution. Without swirling, a local colour change near the drops could be mistaken for the end point.

questions.question:
Sulfuric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide.
H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O
How many moles of sodium hydroxide react with 0.0010 mol of sulfuric acid?
questions.explanation: The equation shows 1 mol of H₂SO₄ reacts with 2 mol of NaOH, so 0.0010 × 2 = 0.0020 mol. 0.00050 mol halves instead of doubling, and 0.0010 mol ignores the 1 : 2 ratio.

questions.question: How should a student read the volume on a burette?
options: At eye level, from the bottom of the meniscus
From above, at the top of the meniscus
From below, at the bottom of the meniscus
At eye level, from the top of the meniscus
markScheme: 1 mark: at eye level, bottom of the meniscus
questions.explanation: Reading at eye level avoids parallax error, and for a colourless solution the bottom of the curved meniscus is read. Reading from above or below gives a value that is too low or too high.

questions.question:
A student did a titration four times.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the mean titre using only the concordant results.
markScheme: 1 mark: identifies 21.15 and 21.25 as concordant (rough and 21.60 excluded)
questions.explanation: 21.15 and 21.25 cm³ are within 0.10 cm³ of each other. The rough titre is excluded and 21.60 cm³ is more than 0.10 cm³ from both. Mean = 42.40 ÷ 2 = 21.20 cm³.

questions.question: Calculate the amount in moles of sodium hydroxide in 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide solution.
questions.explanation: Convert the volume to dm³ first (25.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.0250 dm³), then moles = concentration × volume = 0.100 × 0.0250 = 0.00250 mol. Using 25.0 directly gives 2.5 mol, which is 1000 times too big.

questions.question:
A student titrates potassium hydroxide solution with hydrochloric acid.
HCl + KOH → KCl + H₂O
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the concentration of the hydrochloric acid in mol/dm³.
questions.explanation: Moles of KOH = 0.150 × 0.0250 = 0.00375 mol. The ratio is 1 : 1 so there are 0.00375 mol of HCl in 0.01875 dm³. 0.00375 ÷ 0.01875 = 0.200 mol/dm³.

questions.question:
A student titrates sodium hydroxide solution with sulfuric acid.
H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the concentration of the sulfuric acid in mol/dm³.
questions.explanation: Moles of NaOH = 0.250 × 0.0200 = 0.00500 mol. One H₂SO₄ reacts with two NaOH, so moles of acid = 0.00250 mol. Concentration = 0.00250 ÷ 0.01250 = 0.200 mol/dm³. Forgetting to halve gives 0.400 mol/dm³.

questions.question:
A titration shows that a nitric acid solution has a concentration of 0.200 mol/dm³.
Calculate the concentration of the nitric acid in g/dm³.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): H = 1; N = 14; O = 16
questions.explanation: Mr of HNO₃ = 1 + 14 + 48 = 63. Concentration in g/dm³ = mol/dm³ × Mr = 0.200 × 63 = 12.6 g/dm³.

questions.question:
Sulfuric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide.
H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O
Calculate the volume of 0.0500 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid needed to exactly neutralise 25.0 cm³ of 0.120 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide solution.
Give your answer in cm³.
questions.explanation: Moles of NaOH = 0.00300 mol, so 0.00150 mol of H₂SO₄ is needed. Volume = moles ÷ concentration = 0.00150 ÷ 0.0500 = 0.0300 dm³, which is 30.0 cm³.

questions.question: Name the piece of apparatus used to add acid to the alkali in a titration and measure the volume added.
questions.explanation: A burette has a tap to control the flow, so the acid can be added drop by drop, and its scale reads to 0.05 cm³.

questions.question: Explain why the acid is added drop by drop near the end point of a titration.
acceptedAnswers: so the end point is not overshot
to find the exact volume needed to neutralise
one drop can change the indicator colour
markScheme: 1 mark: to avoid overshooting / adding too much acid
1 mark: so the exact (accurate) volume needed to just neutralise the alkali is found
questions.explanation: Close to the end point a single drop of acid can change the indicator colour. Adding drop by drop means the titre is not too large, so the measured reacting volume is accurate.

questions.question: Explain why a student does a rough titration before the accurate titrations.
acceptedAnswers: to find the approximate end point
so acid can be added quickly then drop by drop near the end point
markScheme: 1 mark: to find the approximate titre / end point
1 mark: so in later runs acid can be added quickly at first and then drop by drop close to this volume
questions.explanation: The rough titration is a guide. Knowing roughly where the end point is lets the student add acid quickly to about 1 cm³ before it, then slowly, saving time and avoiding overshooting.

questions.question: Explain why a titration is repeated until concordant results are obtained.
acceptedAnswers: to check the results are repeatable
markScheme: 1 mark: to show results are repeatable / precise
1 mark: so anomalous results can be identified and excluded from the mean (giving a more accurate value)
questions.explanation: One result could contain a random error. Getting two or more results within 0.10 cm³ shows the method is repeatable, and a mean of concordant results is more reliable than any single titre.

questions.question: Name one indicator that is suitable for a titration between hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide.
questions.explanation: Both give a single sharp colour change. Universal indicator and litmus are not suitable for accurate titrations.

questions.question:
A student rinsed the burette with distilled water but did not rinse it with hydrochloric acid before filling it.
The student used the mean titre to calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide solution.
Explain the effect on the calculated concentration of sodium hydroxide.
markScheme: 1 mark: the acid is diluted by the water
1 mark: so a larger volume (titre) of acid is needed
1 mark: so the moles of acid calculated (using the original concentration) are too high, giving a calculated NaOH concentration that is too high
questions.explanation: The student calculates moles of HCl from the labelled concentration × titre. Because the titre is too large, the calculated moles of HCl, and therefore of NaOH, are too large, so the NaOH concentration comes out too high.

questions.question:
In a titration, the conical flask may be rinsed with distilled water before the alkali is added.
The pipette must be rinsed with the alkali.
Explain why.
acceptedAnswers: water in flask does not change moles of alkali
water in pipette dilutes the alkali so fewer moles
markScheme: 1 mark: water in the flask does not change the number of moles of alkali added (it is already measured by the pipette)
1 mark: water in the pipette would dilute the alkali, so 25.0 cm³ would contain fewer moles of alkali
questions.explanation: The titre depends on the number of moles of alkali in the flask, not on its volume. Extra water in the flask does not change this amount, but water in the pipette reduces the moles delivered.

questions.question: What is meant by the end point of a titration?
acceptedAnswers: acid has just neutralised the alkali
markScheme: 1 mark: the point at which the indicator changes colour (showing the reaction is just complete)
questions.explanation: At the end point all the alkali has just reacted with the acid, which is shown by a permanent colour change of the indicator.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows apparatus used for a titration.
Describe how a student could carry out a titration to find the volume of dilute hydrochloric acid that exactly neutralises 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution.
In your answer you should:
• name the other apparatus used
• explain how accurate and repeatable results would be obtained.

markScheme: Indicative content: rinse burette with the hydrochloric acid and fill it (using a funnel, removed afterwards); record initial reading at eye level from the bottom of the meniscus; use a pipette and pipette filler to transfer 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide into a conical flask; add a few drops of indicator such as phenolphthalein or methyl orange; place flask on a white tile; add acid from the burette while swirling the flask; add acid drop by drop near the end point; stop when the indicator just changes colour permanently (phenolphthalein pink to colourless); record final reading; titre = final − initial; do a rough titration first; repeat until concordant titres within 0.10 cm³; calculate the mean of concordant titres.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed, logically ordered method naming correct apparatus, with dropwise addition near the end point, a correct colour change, repeats to concordant results and calculation of a mean.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a method using a burette, pipette and indicator with a colour change, and some reference to improving accuracy or repeats, though steps may be missing or out of order.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example adding acid to alkali with an indicator until the colour changes.
questions.explanation: Top answers name the pipette, burette, indicator and white tile, describe swirling and dropwise addition, and explain repeating until titres agree within 0.10 cm³ before taking a mean.

questions.question:
A student titrated 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide solution with dilute sulfuric acid.
H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the concentration of the sulfuric acid in mol/dm³ and in g/dm³.
Relative formula mass (Mr): H₂SO₄ = 98

rows: Mean of concordant titres of sulfuric acid

markScheme: 1 mark: 0.100 × 98 = 9.8 g/dm³ (allow error carried forward from an incorrect mol/dm³ value)
questions.explanation: The 1 : 2 ratio means the moles of acid are half the moles of alkali. 0.00125 mol in 0.01250 dm³ gives 0.100 mol/dm³, and multiplying by Mr 98 gives 9.8 g/dm³.

questions.question:
What is the concentration in g/dm³ of a 0.050 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide solution?
Relative formula mass (Mr): NaOH = 40
questions.explanation: g/dm³ = mol/dm³ × Mr = 0.050 × 40 = 2.0 g/dm³. 0.00125 comes from dividing by Mr, and 800 from dividing Mr by 0.050.
